messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kareem is a 54-year-old Iranian-American software engineer who lives alone in a mid-sized city. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 77, indicative of severe posttraumatic stress, and sought help only after a prolonged period of self-managed isolation that had begun to threaten his employment. He describes himself as a private man who had built a quiet, structured life before the assault — a life he no longer recognises.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Kareem was sexually assaulted by a man in a position of institutional authority. The assault occurred at a location he had visited routinely, in a context that carried the implicit weight of hierarchy and power. During the assault, there were sirens audible in the distance — an ambulance passing outside — and the sound became woven into the fabric of the worst minutes of his life. When it was over, no formal action was taken. The perpetrator faced no consequences. Kareem filed no report, in part because he could not imagine being believed, and in part because the authority the perpetrator held made any formal process feel not like protection but like further exposure.

In the months that followed, Kareem came to believe two things with a quiet, corrosive certainty. The first was that what had happened to him was a profound injustice — something fundamentally wrong had been done, and the world had simply continued turning. The second, which lived alongside the first in painful contradiction, was that he himself bore some responsibility; that something in the way he had presented himself, the way he had acted, had made him a target. This self-blame did not absolve his sense of injustice but compounded it, producing a kind of internal deadlock. He had also begun to feel, in a way he struggled to articulate, that his emotional life had been amputated — that whatever had allowed him to feel warmth or ease or ordinary pleasure was simply no longer available to him.

These appraisals drove his behaviour in ways that felt, to him, entirely rational. He stopped going near the location where the assault had occurred, rerouting his commute even when it cost him forty minutes. He avoided any man in uniform — police officers, security guards, military personnel — crossing streets, leaving coffee shops, skipping the pharmacy if a uniformed officer was present. He refused situations that placed him alone with other men. Because he had come to believe the world was genuinely dangerous and that he was a poor judge of safe situations, these precautions felt not like avoidance but like basic competence.

His sense of threat had become totalising. He scanned every room he entered — his open-plan office, the break room, the car park — cataloguing exits, noting who was present, monitoring for anything that felt wrong. He had narrowed the geography of his felt safety to his apartment and, partially, his car. The office had become a place of sustained vigilance rather than work. His productivity dropped sharply, and his manager had raised concerns about his disengagement and missed deadlines, which Kareem registered as confirmation that he was losing his grip on the life he had built.

The avoidance, over time, made everything worse in ways he had not anticipated. By withdrawing from the location, from authority figures, from situations involving other men, he never encountered evidence that he could survive these contexts — and so the threat monitoring intensified rather than abated. Each time he left a space because of a siren or the sight of a uniform, the alarm system reset at a higher baseline. The hypervigilance, in turn, reinforced his belief that he was permanently damaged, that a man who flinched at ambulances and could not sit in a meeting room was not someone who would ever feel normal emotions again. The loop had been running, quietly and relentlessly, for over a year.

What finally brought Kareem to the clinic was a formal performance review in which his employer used the phrase "no longer the person we hired." He heard in it an echo of his own worst fear — that the assault had taken something from him that could not be returned. He arrives hoping, with a tentativeness he cannot quite suppress, that this is not true. What he is most afraid of is that it is.
